aeo.what_is: A brain disorder causing distorted thinking, hallucinations, delusions, and difficulty distinguishing reality from internal experience.

description.main: A chronic mental disorder characterized by persistent disturbances in thought, perception, emotions, and behavior, often including delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, and impaired functioning.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A student starts believing their professors are sending them coded messages through lecture slides and stops attending classes.
Someone hears voices commenting on their actions throughout the day, making it hard to focus at work.
A person becomes convinced their thoughts are being broadcast on the radio and avoids leaving home.
Someone stops showering and changing clothes for weeks, losing motivation to do even basic self-care.
A young adult speaks in jumbled, disconnected sentences that jump from topic to topic without clear logic.
Someone spends days awake, pacing and talking to people others can't see, then sleeps for 20 hours straight.
A person withdraws from family and friends, sitting silently in their room with blank facial expressions for hours.
Someone becomes terrified that neighbors are poisoning their food and refuses to eat anything not prepared by themselves.
description.common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Many people feel shocked, confused, or in denial when first diagnosed, especially if they lack insight into their symptoms. Some experience relief at finally having an explanation for their experiences, while others feel stigmatized or hopeless about their future. Family members may struggle with grief, fear, or guilt. Common initial reactions include: 'This can't be happening to me,' 'Does this mean I'll never be normal again?,' 'Will I be able to work or have relationships?,' and 'What will people think of me?' Over time, with education and support, many develop better understanding and acceptance of their condition as a manageable medical illness.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Two or more of the following, each present for a significant portion of time during a 1-month period (or less if successfully treated), and at least one must be (1), (2), or (3): (1) delusions, (2) hallucinations, (3) disorganized speech, (4) grossly disorganized or catatonic behavior, (5) negative symptoms. B. For a significant portion of the time since onset, level of functioning in one or more major areas (work, interpersonal relations, self-care) is markedly below the level achieved prior to onset. C. Continuous signs of disturbance persist for at least 6 months, with at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms. D. Schizoaffective disorder and mood disorder with psychotic features have been ruled out. E. Not attributable to a substance or another medical condition.
content.temporal_criteria: Diagnosis requires continuous signs of disturbance for at least 6 months, including at least 1 month of active-phase symptoms (delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech). This 6-month period may include prodromal or residual phases where only negative symptoms or attenuated forms of positive symptoms are present. The temporal requirement distinguishes schizophrenia from brief psychotic disorder (less than 1 month) and schizophreniform disorder (1-6 months). If symptoms resolve completely before 6 months with treatment, the diagnosis may be revised. Continuous doesn't mean constant active psychosis—rather, it indicates persistent signs that the illness remains present, even when full psychotic symptoms wax and wane.
content.age_of_onset: Typically late adolescence to early 30s; earlier onset in males (late teens to early 20s) than females (mid-20s to early 30s).
content.prognosis: Variable course; about one-third achieve significant recovery, while others have persistent symptoms and functional impairment. Early intervention and consistent treatment improve long-term outcomes.

circuitry: Dysfunction in fronto-temporal-limbic circuits affecting cognition, perception, and emotional regulation.
neurochemistry: Dopamine dysregulation (mesolimbic hyperactivity linked to positive symptoms; mesocortical hypoactivity linked to negative symptoms).
Glutamatergic NMDA receptor hypofunction and GABAergic deficits.
structural_findings: Reduced gray matter volume in prefrontal and temporal cortices
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Heritability ~80%; environmental factors include prenatal infections, obstetric complications, early cannabis use, and psychosocial stress.

history_psychosocial: Detailed timeline of psychotic symptoms, prodromal changes, and functional decline.
Family psychiatric history and psychosocial stressors.
medical_assessment: Rule out substance-induced psychosis and medical causes (thyroid, neurologic, infectious).
Basic labs, urine toxicology, neuroimaging if indicated.
risk_stratification: Suicide risk is elevated, especially early in illness and after discharge.
Assess aggression risk in acute psychosis.
differential_diagnosis: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
evaluation.team_and_process: Multidisciplinary approach with psychiatry, psychology, social work, and occupational therapy.

core: Negative symptoms (avolition, alogia, anhedonia, flat affect)

severity_levels.mild: Symptoms present but partially compensated; functioning impaired but some independence maintained.
severity_levels.moderate: Ongoing symptoms with significant impairment in work, social, and self-care domains.
severity_levels.severe: Severe psychosis or negative symptoms with profound functional disability.

biological: Family history of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders

impact_on_life.school_work: Decline in academic/work performance due to disorganization, cognitive deficits, and social withdrawal.
impact_on_life.social: Relationship strain from odd behavior, paranoia, or withdrawal.
impact_on_life.medical: Side effects from antipsychotic medications (metabolic syndrome, movement disorders).
impact_on_life.emotional: Frustration, hopelessness, or lack of motivation.

medications: Antipsychotics: first-generation (haloperidol, fluphenazine) and second-generation (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole, clozapine for treatment-resistant cases)
neuromodulation: ECT for severe catatonia or depression

treatment_goals: Reduce severity and frequency of psychotic episodes.
Improve functioning and quality of life.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Attributing early psychotic symptoms to depression, anxiety, or substance use without longitudinal assessment.
Failing to recognize subtle prodromal changes.
overdiagnosis_factors: Misinterpreting transient stress-induced psychosis as schizophrenia.
Confusing mood disorder with psychotic features for primary psychotic disorder.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Schizophrenia is frequently misdiagnosed because psychotic symptoms appear in many conditions. Early in the illness course, brief reactive psychosis from severe stress, substance-induced psychosis (especially from cannabis, stimulants, or hallucinogens), or mood episodes with psychotic features may look identical to schizophrenia but have different trajectories and treatments. Schizoaffective disorder is particularly challenging to distinguish because it requires careful longitudinal tracking of mood versus psychotic symptoms. Medical conditions like autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid disorders, or temporal lobe epilepsy can mimic schizophrenia. Additionally, autism spectrum disorder, severe PTSD with dissociation, or borderline personality disorder with transient psychotic symptoms are sometimes confused with schizophrenia. Accurate diagnosis requires at least 6 months of observation, thorough substance use history, medical workup, and careful assessment of mood symptoms' timing relative to psychosis.

specifiers.first_episode: First episode of psychosis meeting full criteria.
specifiers.multiple_episodes: Two or more episodes, with or without residual symptoms.
specifiers.continuous: Symptoms meet criteria throughout the majority of the illness course.

warning_signs: Progressive social withdrawal and decline in functioning.
Emergence of fixed false beliefs or hallucinations.
Marked disorganization in speech or behavior.

adolescents: Social isolation, academic decline, odd beliefs; may have more abrupt onset.
adults: Chronic course with periods of exacerbation and remission.
older_adults: Possible late-onset cases; more likely to have paranoid symptoms and less severe negative symptoms.

first_person_statements: Sometimes I can't tell if the voices I hear are coming from outside or inside my head—it's like reality keeps shifting and I don't know what's real anymore.
The hardest part isn't the hallucinations, it's the emptiness afterward—I can go days without feeling anything, not wanting to do anything, just existing in this gray fog.
People think I'm being difficult when I don't answer their questions, but my thoughts get so jumbled that by the time I form a sentence, I've forgotten what we were talking about.
I had to drop out of college because I became convinced my roommates were stealing my thoughts at night—I know now it wasn't real, but at the time it was absolutely terrifying.
The medication helps with the paranoia, but I miss feeling like myself—sometimes I wonder if I'll ever get back to who I was before this started.
My family doesn't understand why I can't just 'snap out of it' or 'try harder'—they think I'm lazy, but some days getting out of bed feels impossible.

real_life_examples: Marcus, a 22-year-old engineering student, began his junior year noticing he could hear faint whispers when no one was around. Over several weeks, the whispers became clear voices—multiple people discussing him, sometimes mocking, sometimes warning him of danger. He started believing his lab partners were government agents monitoring him through the computer cameras. His speech became tangential, jumping between conspiracy theories and engineering concepts without clear connections. He stopped attending classes, stopped showering, and spent days in his dorm room taping over all electronic devices. His roommate found him trying to extract a 'tracking chip' from his arm with a knife. After hospitalization and starting antipsychotic medication, the voices quieted but didn't disappear entirely, and he struggled with profound apathy and difficulty organizing his thoughts enough to return to school.

Yuki, 28, had always been shy but functioned well as a graphic designer until she gradually became convinced her co-workers could hear her thoughts. She began wearing headphones constantly, believing they blocked the 'thought broadcasting.' She stopped speaking in meetings because she felt everyone already knew what she would say. At home, she heard her deceased grandmother's voice telling her she was special and chosen for an important mission she didn't yet understand. Her designs became increasingly bizarre and symbolic, filled with hidden messages only she understood. She lost track of time, sometimes working for 36 hours straight, other times lying in bed for days unable to move or care for herself. Her apartment became cluttered with notebooks filled with elaborate diagrams connecting unrelated world events. When her sister visited and found her malnourished and dehydrated, Yuki couldn't explain what had been happening—her memories of the past months felt fragmented and dreamlike.

James, 19, started college as a popular, outgoing freshman but by winter break had become almost unrecognizable. His parents noticed he rarely made eye contact, spoke in a monotone voice, and his responses to questions seemed vaguely related but not quite on topic. He mentioned casually that he'd discovered he could control the weather with his thoughts and had been preventing hurricanes. When they expressed concern, he became agitated, accusing them of being 'part of it' without explaining what 'it' was. Back at school, his roommate reported James stood motionless facing the wall for hours, occasionally laughing at nothing, and had written hundreds of pages about mathematics proving he was God's chosen prophet. He stopped eating food others prepared, convinced it was poisoned. His academic work shifted from coherent essays to word salads mixing philosophy, religion, and personal delusions. Campus police found him standing in a fountain at 3 AM, claiming he needed to purify himself before the 'truth revealing.'

Linda, 31, had worked successfully as a teacher for eight years before the gradual onset of symptoms. She began experiencing visual distortions—students' faces seemed to morph and blur. She heard children's voices calling her name in empty hallways. She became convinced the principal was running a child trafficking ring and spent evenings compiling 'evidence' from innocent interactions she'd witnessed. Her lesson plans became increasingly disorganized and tangential. She stopped grading papers, claiming the handwriting contained hidden messages about her. She lost interest in hobbies she'd loved, stopped seeing friends, and spent weekends sitting on her couch staring blankly at turned-off television screens. Her speech became sparse and flat. When concerned colleagues asked if she was okay, she either didn't respond or made cryptic comments about 'seeing through the illusion.' She missed multiple days of work without calling in, later unable to explain where the time had gone or why she hadn't noticed the days passing.

David, 25, a musician, first noticed something was wrong when he became convinced his bandmates were communicating with aliens and excluding him from secret meetings. He heard music constantly—beautiful, complex symphonies no one else could hear, which he frantically tried to transcribe. His transcriptions became increasingly chaotic and unreadable. He believed he'd been chosen to translate alien messages through music and spent days without sleep trying to complete this 'mission.' His speech became pressured and disorganized, jumping between topics: aliens, music theory, childhood memories, government conspiracies, all woven together in ways that made sense to him but confused everyone else. He stopped paying rent, stopped eating regularly, and lost significant weight. His apartment filled with hundreds of pages of 'translations'—gibberish interspersed with musical notation and drawings of geometric patterns he claimed were alien language. When his girlfriend tried to help, he accused her of being an alien imposter replacing the real version of her, unable to recognize that his perception had become completely untethered from reality.

comparisons.key_difference: In schizophrenia, psychotic symptoms persist even when mood is normal; in schizoaffective disorder, major mood episodes (depression or mania) are present for the majority of the illness duration and overlap significantly with psychotic symptoms. If someone only has delusions during depressive or manic episodes, it's a mood disorder with psychotic features, not schizophrenia.
comparisons.clinical_significance: Treatment for schizoaffective disorder typically requires both antipsychotics and mood stabilizers or antidepressants, while schizophrenia focuses primarily on antipsychotics. The prognosis for schizoaffective disorder often falls between mood disorders and schizophrenia.

comparisons.key_difference: Brief psychotic disorder involves sudden onset of psychotic symptoms lasting less than 1 month with eventual full return to baseline functioning. Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of continuous disturbance (including prodromal or residual symptoms) and typically doesn't involve complete return to previous functioning.
comparisons.clinical_significance: Brief psychotic disorder often follows severe stress or trauma and may not require long-term antipsychotic treatment, whereas schizophrenia typically requires ongoing medication management to prevent relapse.

comparisons.key_difference: Substance-induced psychosis begins during or shortly after substance intoxication or withdrawal and resolves within days to weeks of abstinence. Schizophrenia symptoms persist independently of substance use, though substances may worsen them. Careful history and observation during abstinence periods are essential for distinction.
comparisons.clinical_significance: If psychosis resolves completely with sustained abstinence from substances (particularly stimulants, cannabis, or hallucinogens), schizophrenia diagnosis should not be made. Some individuals with substance-induced psychosis may later develop schizophrenia, requiring longitudinal monitoring.

comparisons.key_difference: Delusional disorder involves non-bizarre, fixed false beliefs (like being followed, having a disease, or being deceived by a spouse) without prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms. Apart from the delusion's impact, functioning isn't markedly impaired. Schizophrenia involves multiple symptom domains and broader functional decline.
comparisons.clinical_significance: Delusional disorder is rarer and typically has later onset. People with delusional disorder often maintain jobs and relationships except where the delusion directly interferes, while schizophrenia causes more pervasive impairment across life domains.

faqs.question: Does schizophrenia mean someone has a 'split personality'?
faqs.answer: No, this is a common misconception. Schizophrenia doesn't mean split or multiple personalities—that's dissociative identity disorder, a completely different condition. The 'split' in schizophrenia refers to a disconnection from reality, where thoughts, perceptions, and emotions don't align with what's actually happening. People with schizophrenia have one personality but may experience distorted thinking, hallucinations, and difficulty distinguishing internal experiences from external reality.

faqs.question: Are people with schizophrenia dangerous or violent?
faqs.answer: The vast majority of people with schizophrenia are not violent and are more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators. Media portrayals dramatically exaggerate this risk. When violence does occur, it's usually related to untreated acute psychosis, substance use, or past history of violence—not the diagnosis itself. Most people with schizophrenia who receive treatment live peacefully in their communities. This stigma causes tremendous harm and prevents people from seeking help.

faqs.question: Will I have to take medication for the rest of my life?
faqs.answer: Most people with schizophrenia benefit from long-term antipsychotic medication to prevent relapse. Research shows that discontinuing medication significantly increases the risk of psychotic episodes returning, often more severely. However, treatment plans are individualized—some people eventually reduce doses or try medication holidays under close medical supervision. The goal is finding the minimum effective dose that controls symptoms while minimizing side effects. Medication decisions should always be made collaboratively with your psychiatrist, weighing relapse risk against quality of life.

faqs.question: Can people with schizophrenia work or go to school?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people with schizophrenia maintain employment or pursue education, especially with early treatment and ongoing support. Success often depends on symptom severity, cognitive functioning, workplace accommodations, and access to vocational rehabilitation. Some people work full-time in competitive employment; others benefit from supported employment programs that provide job coaching and flexible arrangements. Educational accommodations like reduced course loads, extended deadlines, or note-taking assistance can help students succeed. Recovery is possible, though the path varies for each person.

faqs.question: What causes schizophrenia?
faqs.answer: Schizophrenia results from complex interactions between genetic vulnerability and environmental factors. It's highly heritable (about 80%), but having a family member with schizophrenia doesn't guarantee you'll develop it—most people with genetic risk never become ill. Environmental factors that increase risk include prenatal infections or malnutrition, birth complications, childhood trauma, cannabis use during adolescence, urban upbringing, and severe psychosocial stress. Brain differences in structure, chemistry (especially dopamine and glutamate systems), and neural circuits are found in schizophrenia, but no single cause has been identified. It's a brain disorder, not caused by bad parenting or personal weakness.

faqs.question: How can I tell if I'm developing schizophrenia?
faqs.answer: Early warning signs (prodromal symptoms) often appear months or years before full psychosis and include: gradual social withdrawal, decline in school or work performance, unusual thoughts or suspiciousness, perceptual changes (things seeming strange or distorted), difficulty concentrating, sleep problems, and emotional flatness. These symptoms are subtle and non-specific—many people experience them without developing schizophrenia. If you're concerned, especially if you have family history or are in the typical age range (late teens to early 30s), see a mental health professional for evaluation. Early intervention improves outcomes significantly.

faqs.question: What's the difference between positive and negative symptoms?
faqs.answer: Positive symptoms are experiences added to normal functioning: hallucinations (seeing, hearing, or sensing things not there), delusions (fixed false beliefs), disorganized speech, and disorganized or catatonic behavior. Negative symptoms represent diminished normal functioning: reduced emotional expression (flat affect), lack of motivation (avolition), reduced speech (alogia), inability to experience pleasure (anhedonia), and social withdrawal. Medications typically work better for positive symptoms; negative symptoms are often more resistant to treatment and more strongly impact long-term functioning. Addressing negative symptoms often requires combining medication with psychotherapy, social skills training, and rehabilitation.

faqs.question: Can schizophrenia be cured?
faqs.answer: There's currently no cure for schizophrenia, but it's highly treatable, and many people achieve significant recovery. About one-third of people have good outcomes with minimal symptoms and functional recovery, one-third have moderate symptoms requiring ongoing treatment, and one-third have more persistent symptoms. Recovery doesn't always mean symptom-free—it often means learning to manage symptoms, maintain relationships, work or study, and live meaningfully. Early intervention, consistent medication use, therapy, family support, and avoiding substance use all improve outcomes. Research continues toward better treatments and potentially preventive interventions.

faqs.question: Do the voices people hear sound real?
faqs.answer: To the person experiencing them, auditory hallucinations usually sound completely real—as clear and external as actual voices. They might hear single or multiple voices, male or female, familiar or unfamiliar. The voices might comment on actions, converse with each other, command behaviors, or criticize. Sometimes they're whispers; other times they're loud. Some people can distinguish hallucinations from reality with effort; others cannot. This is why 'just ignore the voices' isn't helpful advice—they can be extremely compelling and distressing. Treatment with antipsychotic medication can reduce or eliminate hallucinations for many people.

faqs.question: What should I do if someone I love is experiencing psychosis?
faqs.answer: Stay calm and avoid arguing about their beliefs or perceptions—you can't logic someone out of delusions or hallucinations. Listen without judgment, validate their feelings ('I can see you're frightened') without confirming delusions ('Yes, the FBI is after you'). Ensure their immediate safety—remove dangerous items if they're agitated. Encourage professional help gently; if they refuse and are in danger, you may need to call emergency services or explore involuntary evaluation options depending on local laws. After the crisis, support treatment adherence, learn about schizophrenia, consider family therapy, and take care of your own mental health. Organizations like NAMI offer resources and support groups for families.

faqs.question: Will I be able to have relationships and a family?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people with schizophrenia maintain meaningful relationships, marry, and have children. Relationships may require extra effort due to symptoms like social withdrawal, emotional flatness, or cognitive difficulties, but they're absolutely possible. Open communication with partners about symptoms and needs helps. For those considering having children, genetic counseling can address hereditary concerns—while risk is elevated if a parent has schizophrenia (about 10-15% for offspring), most children will not develop the condition. Pregnancy planning should involve discussion with your psychiatrist about medication safety. Building a life with relationships you value is a realistic goal with treatment and support.

faqs.question: Why do antipsychotic medications cause weight gain and other side effects?
faqs.answer: Antipsychotics work by affecting brain neurotransmitter systems, particularly dopamine, but they also impact other systems throughout the body. Weight gain occurs because some antipsychotics affect metabolism, increase appetite, and alter how the body processes glucose and fats—particularly second-generation antipsychotics like olanzapine and clozapine. Other side effects include sedation, movement problems (especially with older antipsychotics), sexual dysfunction, and increased prolactin. Not everyone experiences all side effects, and different medications have different profiles. Working with your psychiatrist to find the medication that balances symptom control with tolerable side effects is crucial. Lifestyle interventions, medication adjustments, or adding other medications can sometimes manage side effects.

faqs.question: What's the difference between first-generation and second-generation antipsychotics?
faqs.answer: First-generation antipsychotics (FGAs, 'typical' antipsychotics) like haloperidol were developed in the 1950s and primarily block dopamine D2 receptors. They effectively treat positive symptoms but commonly cause movement side effects (extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia). Second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs, 'atypical' antipsychotics) like risperidone, olanzapine, and aripiprazole were developed later and affect both dopamine and serotonin systems. They have lower risk of movement problems but higher risk of metabolic side effects (weight gain, diabetes). Neither class is universally better—choice depends on individual symptom profile, side effect tolerance, and personal response. Clozapine, an SGA, is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia due to serious side effects but is often the most effective.

faqs.question: Can cannabis use cause schizophrenia?
faqs.answer: Cannabis doesn't directly cause schizophrenia in everyone who uses it, but it significantly increases risk, especially with heavy use, high-potency products, and use during adolescence when the brain is still developing. People with genetic vulnerability to schizophrenia are particularly at risk—cannabis use may trigger onset in those predisposed. Studies show cannabis use is associated with earlier age of onset and worse outcomes. Some people experience temporary cannabis-induced psychosis that resolves with abstinence; others develop persistent schizophrenia. If you have family history of psychotic disorders, avoiding cannabis is strongly recommended. If you have schizophrenia, continued cannabis use typically worsens symptoms and interferes with treatment.

faqs.question: What happens during a psychiatric hospitalization for psychosis?
faqs.answer: Hospitalization provides a safe, structured environment for stabilization during acute psychosis. Upon admission, you'll undergo medical and psychiatric evaluation. Staff will monitor your safety, ensure you eat and sleep, and start or adjust medications. Treatment includes medication management, individual check-ins with psychiatrists and nurses, group therapy, and activities. The length of stay varies—typically days to weeks—depending on symptom severity and response to treatment. The goal is stabilization, not cure: reducing acute symptoms enough for safe discharge with outpatient follow-up. Involuntary hospitalization can occur if someone is dangerous to themselves or others and refuses voluntary admission. After discharge, connecting quickly with outpatient care is critical for preventing relapse.

faqs.question: How does schizophrenia affect cognitive functioning?
faqs.answer: Most people with schizophrenia experience some cognitive difficulties, even when psychotic symptoms are controlled. Common problems include: working memory (holding information in mind), processing speed (how quickly you think), attention and concentration, executive functioning (planning, organizing, problem-solving), and verbal learning and memory. These difficulties can impact daily functioning—remembering appointments, following complex instructions, multitasking, or learning new information. Cognitive deficits often appear before psychotic symptoms and persist throughout illness. They're usually not severe enough to qualify as dementia but can affect work and school performance significantly. Cognitive remediation therapy and compensatory strategies (using calendars, breaking tasks into steps, reducing distractions) can help. Some medications may slightly improve cognition, though none specifically target these symptoms.

faqs.question: Is it normal to still hear voices even on medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, for many people, antipsychotics reduce hallucinations but don't eliminate them completely. Some continue hearing voices at lower volume or frequency, or develop strategies to manage them even when present. Treatment success doesn't always mean total symptom absence—it often means reducing symptoms to manageable levels that allow functioning. If voices remain distressing or command dangerous actions, medication adjustment should be discussed with your psychiatrist. Some people benefit from switching medications, increasing dosage (within safe limits), or adding augmentation strategies. CBT for psychosis can help develop coping strategies for persistent voices. Complete resolution is possible for some but not all people; meaningful improvement rather than perfection is often the realistic goal.

faqs.question: What's the role of therapy in treating schizophrenia?
faqs.answer: While medication is essential for managing psychotic symptoms, therapy addresses many aspects medication doesn't touch. Cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (CBTp) helps people understand and cope with symptoms, challenge distorted beliefs, and reduce distress from persistent hallucinations. Social skills training improves communication and relationship abilities. Family therapy educates families and improves communication. Cognitive remediation targets thinking and memory problems. Supportive therapy helps process the diagnosis, build coping strategies, and work toward goals. Many people benefit from combined medication and therapy—medication reduces symptom intensity while therapy helps rebuild functioning and quality of life. Therapy alone isn't effective for schizophrenia, but it's an important part of comprehensive treatment.

faqs.question: What's the likelihood of passing schizophrenia to my children?
faqs.answer: If one parent has schizophrenia, each child has approximately 10-15% risk of developing it—significantly higher than the general population risk of about 1%, but still meaning most children will not develop schizophrenia. If both parents have schizophrenia, risk increases to about 40-50%. Having a sibling with schizophrenia confers about 10% risk. These are probabilities, not certainties—genetic vulnerability requires environmental triggers to manifest. Many people with family history never develop psychotic disorders. If you're concerned about hereditary risk, genetic counseling can provide personalized risk assessment and help with family planning decisions. Advances in early intervention mean that even if children develop psychosis, earlier treatment significantly improves outcomes.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm having a relapse?
faqs.answer: Early warning signs of relapse often mirror prodromal symptoms but appear in someone previously stabilized: sleep disturbances, social withdrawal, suspiciousness, difficulty concentrating, loss of interest in activities, reduced self-care, unusual thoughts, or perceptual changes. Some people experience the same pattern each time (like first hearing whispering, then voices becoming clearer). Monitoring for personal early warning signs—ideally with help from family or friends who notice changes—allows for early intervention. If you notice warning signs, contact your psychiatrist immediately; medication adjustment or increased support can often prevent full relapse. Missing medication doses, using substances, experiencing major stress, or stopping therapy are common relapse triggers. Having a relapse prevention plan identifying your warning signs and action steps is extremely valuable.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek urgent evaluation for psychosis, inability to care for self, or suicidal/homicidal thoughts.
